The name

Saturday, 20 December 2030, evening. Ioana is eight months pregnant. She and Julien are sitting on the sofa with a long list of names. Rose-Hélène is asleep. The baby is due at the beginning of January and they still haven’t chosen the name.
Right. Let’s recap. I’m looking for a name that’s simple, that can be pronounced in French, Romanian and Spanish, and that isn’t shared by half the crèche.
And if it’s a girl? We said we didn’t want to know.
For a girl I’ve found one: Elena, like my mother. There’s no name I like better. And it works everywhere.
Agreed on Elena. Your mother will cry for a week. And for a boy?
For a boy… I’ve had one in mind for a long time. But I’m not sure there’s anyone who could carry it without it weighing too heavily.
(smiles) I think I know which one. It’s the only name that has meaning in our story.
Henri.
Henri. But we’d have to ask Odile. She’s the only person who really has the right to say yes or no.
And Isabelle. He was her father.
You’re right. And as a middle name? I’m looking for a name that recalls your family.
Ion. Like my grandfather, the best dancer in the village. Henri-Ion Moreau.
Henri for the waltz, Ion for the hora. It’s the most danceable name I’ve ever heard.
(laughs, then puts her hand on her belly) He moved. I think he agrees. Or else it’s a girl protesting.

1. Relative clauses expressing a search
When you look for something you DON’T know exists, the verb in the relative clause is in the SUBJUNCTIVE. When you talk about something that certainly EXISTS, use the indicative:
Thing sought (subjunctive)
Real thing (indicative)
Je cherche un prénom qui soit simple.
J’ai trouvé un prénom qui est simple.
Je cherche quelqu’un qui sache siffler.
Je connais quelqu’un qui sait siffler.
Il veut une maison qui ait un jardin.
Il a une maison qui a un jardin.
English shows a similar contrast with “should / could”: “a name that would be simple” vs “a name that is simple”. Think: is it real or only wished for?
2. After a superlative and “le seul”
After a superlative or after “le seul, l’unique, le premier, le dernier”, the subjunctive stresses the exceptional nature:
It’s the only name that has meaning in our story.
She’s the only person who can say yes.
He’s the first child born in the new year.
With the indicative, the sentence is just an objective statement: “C’est le seul qui est venu” (= only he came). With the subjunctive it is more subjective, more careful.

On Sunday 21 December, Ioana and Julien crossed the landing together to knock on Odile’s door. They had rehearsed what they were going to say the evening before, like two pupils before an exam. Odile received them in her armchair by the window, a blanket on her knees. The bronchitis had gone, but it had left behind a tiredness that nothing seemed able to chase away.

Ioana sat on the stool beside her. Julien stayed standing, hands in his pockets, like a teenager. Ioana explained that they had finally chosen the names. Elena, if it was a girl. And if it was a boy… She hesitated. Then she said it, very softly: “Henri. But only if you agree. You’re the only person who can tell us yes.”

Odile didn’t answer for a long moment. She turned her head towards the window, towards the grey roofs of the Croix-Rousse. Her hands tightened on the blanket. Ioana began to regret asking. Perhaps it was too much, perhaps the name belonged to Odile and nobody else. Then Odile turned back. She was crying, but she was smiling.

“Do you know what he used to say about his name?” she asked. “He said it was a king’s name, too serious for a sailor. He would have laughed. He’d have said the poor child would have to wear a crown.” She wiped her eyes with the corner of the blanket. “Yes. I agree. On one condition: that he learns to whistle. A Henri who doesn’t whistle doesn’t exist.”

That same evening they called Isabelle in Paris. She listened without interrupting, then there was a silence on the line. “You know,” she said at last, “I’ve always regretted not having a child I could name after my father. I thought the name would stop with me.” She took a deep breath. “Thank you. It’s the most beautiful present anyone has ever given me.”

The next day Elena arrived from Iași on the morning flight. She had decided to come before Christmas, in case the baby was in a hurry. She had brought two suitcases: one for her clothes, and one for the baby, full of little hats knitted by the grandmother, tiny socks and a blanket embroidered with ie patterns. Dan would come later, for the christening, if work allowed.

On 23 December, Odile turned eighty. She had forbidden anyone to organise a party. Of course, nobody listened to her. At five o’clock her little sitting room was full: Ioana, Julien, Rose-Hélène, Elena, Radu and Lucia, Mrs Roux, Théo, Mr Fournier with a bunch of holly sprigs, and Isabelle, who had come from Paris as a surprise.

Théo had brought a present he had spent a month preparing in secret: a recording of the La Duchère orchestra playing the waltz, but with a silence at the third verse. A silence of eight bars. “That’s your place,” he explained to Odile. “The third verse is yours to whistle. Always. Even when you’re not there.” Odile had to sit down.

Mrs Roux had brought a little tin box, rusty at the edges. Inside was a clarinet reed, yellowed with age, wrapped in a handkerchief embroidered with two letters: “L. R.”. “It’s Lucien’s last reed,” she explained. “I’ve kept it for twenty years. It’s no good for anything any more. But I wanted it to go to someone who knows what it means to wait.” Odile took it in her hands like a relic.

They listened to the recording together. At the third verse, when the silence came, Odile whistled. Her voice was weaker than before, a little shaky, but she held the eight bars to the end. When the orchestra came back in, everyone applauded. Mrs Roux declared it was the most beautiful concert she had ever heard in a sitting room.

On Christmas Eve they had dinner at Ioana and Julien’s. Pierre, Brigitte and Manon had come from Annecy with a Yule log and a brioche. Odile crossed the landing in a velvet dress, on Isabelle’s arm. Elena had cooked sarmale following the grandmother’s recipe, and Brigitte had roasted a turkey. Nobody managed to finish either.

Around nine, the grandmother called from Iași by video, with the whole village behind her, or almost: the neighbours had come to sing colinde, Romanian Christmas carols, in front of her door. She turned the phone towards them, and for five minutes the living room on rue d’Austerlitz filled with the voices of men and women singing in the snow, two thousand kilometres away.

Pierre Moreau, who had never heard colinde, asked Elena to translate the words for him. Elena tried, then gave up. “They can’t be translated,” she said. “They talk about a star, a child, and people waiting at a door.” Pierre nodded, deeply moved. “Then it’s the same story as ours,” he replied. Nobody could think of a way to contradict him.

Rose-Hélène, who would turn three in March, had been given a little wooden piano. She spent the evening playing the first three notes of the waltz, again and again, with one finger, stopping every two minutes to press her ear against her mother’s belly. “He’s listening,” she announced each time. “Baby Waltz is listening.” Nobody had the heart to contradict her.

The week between Christmas and New Year was strangely calm. Julien had taken leave, as he had required in his contract. Amina had forbidden him to answer emails. “If you so much as open your inbox,” she wrote, “I’ll know.” Julien didn’t dare check whether it was true. He spent his days putting the cot back together and painting the little room yellow.

On the evening of 31 December they didn’t go out. They watched the fireworks from the living-room window, above the roofs, with Rose-Hélène asleep in Julien’s arms. Across the landing they could see Odile’s silhouette at her window, looking at the same sky. At midnight she raised her hand, as if to clink glasses with them through the pane.

On 2 January, late in the day, it began to snow. It was the first snow of the winter, big slow flakes falling silently on the Croix-Rousse. Rose-Hélène pressed her nose to the window, enchanted. Ioana, sitting on the sofa, put her hand on her belly and said, very calmly: “Julien. I think it’s tonight.”

Julien, who had conducted orchestras in front of two thousand people, lost all ability to think. He looked for his keys for five minutes while they were in his hand. He put his coat on inside out. He called a taxi, then called back to check he had given the right address. Elena, on the other hand, had had the suitcase packed, just in case, since 22 December.

On the landing, Odile’s door opened. She was there, in her dressing gown, her hair loose, woken by the noise. She looked at Ioana, then at Julien with his coat inside out, and understood everything. She said nothing. She just took Ioana’s hand, squeezed it very hard, then whistled three notes, very quietly. For luck.

The taxi drove slowly through the snowy streets to the Croix-Rousse maternity hospital, the same one where Rose-Hélène had been born almost three years earlier. Arriving at midnight, they were welcomed by a midwife of about fifty, Mrs Leroy, who had an impressive calm and a very gentle voice. She looked at Julien and smiled. “You,” she said, “are going to breathe with Madame.”

Julien tried. He really tried. But conductor though he was, he couldn’t keep the breathing rhythm for more than three minutes. Ioana, between two contractions, ended up laughing. “You conducted better at the Philharmonie,” she said. Mrs Leroy suggested another solution: “Sing her something. Something in three-four time.”

So Julien hummed Henri’s waltz. Softly, close to Ioana’s ear, holding her hand. He hummed it for two hours, again and again, slowing down when the pain came and picking up again when it went. Mrs Leroy said later that it was the first time, in thirty years in the job, that a birth had had its own soundtrack.

Henri-Ion Moreau was born on Friday 3 January 2031, at four in the morning. He weighed three kilos four hundred, measured fifty-one centimetres, and cried very loudly, straight away, as if he had something important to announce. Mrs Leroy laid him on Ioana’s chest. Julien, who was no longer humming anything, was crying silently.

“It’s a boy,” said Mrs Leroy. “Do you have a name?” Ioana looked at the little red wrinkled face, the clenched fists, the eyes still closed. “Henri,” she replied. “Henri-Ion.” The baby stopped crying all at once, as if he had recognised his name. Mrs Leroy raised her eyebrows. “Well, he seems to agree.”

At eight in the morning it was still snowing. Elena arrived with Rose-Hélène, bundled up in a pink coat, a hat knitted by the grandmother on her head. And behind them, on Isabelle’s arm, was Odile. She had insisted on coming, despite the snow, despite her tiredness, despite everyone’s protests. “Even if there were a metre of snow,” she said, “I would come.”

Rose-Hélène tiptoed up to the transparent cot. She looked at her little brother for a long time, very seriously, the way you examine a present you’re not yet sure about. Then she took Henri’s harmonica out of her pocket, the one she never parted with, and blew three notes, very softly, next to his head.

And Henri-Ion opened his eyes. For the first time. He looked in the direction of the sound, with those blurry dark eyes of newborns, who can still hardly see anything. Rose-Hélène turned to the adults, triumphant. “He heard,” she said. “I told you. He understands music. He’s the only baby who understands music.”

Then it was Odile’s turn. Ioana picked up the baby and laid him carefully in her wrinkled arms. Odile looked at him without saying anything. The little one grabbed her finger and squeezed it very hard, with the astonishing strength of the very small. Odile smiled. “Hello, Henri,” she murmured. “It was time you came back.”

Then she whistled, very quietly, the eight bars of the third verse. Her place. The baby in her arms fell asleep before the end, her finger still clasped in his little hand. Isabelle, standing behind her mother, put her hands on her shoulders. Nobody in the room spoke for a long time. The snow kept falling beyond the window.

Julien went out into the corridor to call his father in Annecy. Pierre picked up on the first ring; he was already in his bakery, his hands in the flour, as every morning for forty years. When Julien told him the name, there was a long silence. Then Pierre said: “Henri. That’s good. Your grandfather Marcel would have liked that. He always said a child should bear the name of someone who knew how to wait.”

Nathalie came by in the late morning with a present from the whole firm: a little wooden model, made by Radu and Chloé in their lunch breaks. It was the Hélène Morel hall, in miniature, with a window in the roof that really opened. Inside they had fitted a music box. When you opened the window, it played the first three notes of the waltz. Rose-Hélène refused to let go of it for an hour.

The rest of the day was an avalanche of phone calls. The grandmother called from Iași at nine to say she had already known, because she had dreamed of fish all night. Dan took the phone to declare, in the French of his old textbook: “Congratulations on this happy event.” Elena cried in both languages.

From Seville, don Manuel played a little tune on the guitar over the phone, an Andalusian lullaby he had improvised for the occasion. Lucia and Radu arrived at noon with an enormous bouquet and a card signed by the sixty La Duchère children. On the card, Inès had added a sentence: “When he wants, I’ll teach him the clarinet. As long as he’s patient.”

Around two in the afternoon, Julien got a message from Amina. It was very short. “Congratulations, Mr Moreau. Welcome, Henri-Ion.” Then, a minute later, a second message: “This is an emotion. I own it.” Julien showed the message to Ioana, who laughed so loudly that Mrs Leroy came to check everything was all right.

On Monday 6 January, Julien went to the town hall of the 4th arrondissement to register the birth. Behind the counter he found a familiar face: Théo’s mother. She had registered Rose-Hélène’s birth almost three years earlier, and had prepared Julien and Ioana’s wedding before that. She smiled when she saw Julien come in. “I’m starting to know your whole family,” she said.

She wrote the name carefully, checking the spelling: Henri, with an i, like the one on the plaque of the Henri Bernard hall at Fourvière. Ion, without an h, like the Romanian grandfather’s. Then she looked up. “Henri-Ion. That’s a name with a story, isn’t it?” Julien smiled. “It’s the only name that can tell ours.”

That evening on rue d’Austerlitz, everyone was asleep. Ioana, exhausted, had fallen asleep at nine. Rose-Hélène was sleeping with the harmonica under her pillow. Elena was snoring gently in Odile’s guest room. Only Julien was still up, with Henri-Ion in his arms, who didn’t want to sleep. He paced up and down the living room, rocking him.

It was then that he heard it, through the door across the landing: the first three notes of the waltz, whistled very quietly. Odile wasn’t asleep either. Julien went up to the door, the baby on his shoulder, and whistled the next three notes. Then he waited. Behind the door, Odile whistled the whole third verse.

When she had finished, Julien looked at his son. Henri-Ion was asleep at last, his mouth half open, one hand resting on his father’s shirt collar. Outside, the snow covered the roofs of the Croix-Rousse, the banks of the Saône, the benches of the Parc de la Tête d’Or and, somewhere in a greenhouse, nine little lime trees waiting for spring to set off in their turn.

Faire-part de naissance

Rose-Hélène is delighted to announce the birth of her little brother, Henri-Ion Moreau, on Friday 3 January 2031, at four in the morning, at the Croix-Rousse maternity hospital. He weighs three kilos four hundred and measures fifty-one centimetres.

His parents, Ioana and Julien, wanted a name with meaning. They chose Henri, in tribute to a sailor who wrote a waltz in 1962, and Ion, in tribute to a great-grandfather who was the best dancer in his village.

Before choosing, they asked permission from the only two people who could give it: Odile Bernard, who was Henri’s wife for more than fifty years, and Isabelle Bernard, his daughter. Both said yes, in tears.

Henri-Ion was born on a snowy night, the first of the winter in Lyon. Having arrived at the maternity ward around midnight, his mother gave birth in four hours. His father, conductor though he was, couldn’t keep the breathing rhythm.

His big sister, who is almost three, came to see him that very morning. She played him three notes on the harmonica, and he opened his eyes. Since then she has claimed he is the most beautiful baby she has ever seen, and the only one who really understands music.
The parents thank the midwife, the most patient they have ever met, as well as all those who supported them. They ask you not to send presents. If you absolutely wish to do something, plant a tree.
